opening_message: There's a vine on a trellis by the porch that we've mostly just left alone, and it gets these nice purple flower clusters in the spring. Should I keep letting it grow there, or is it something I ought to get rid of?

slots.name: seed_pod_texture
slots.value: There's a couple of old dried-up seed pods on it from last year, and they're smooth, not fuzzy at all.
slots.description: Smooth seed pods match native American wisteria; the invasive Chinese wisteria's pods are velvety by comparison -- the key confirming ID feature here.

slots.name: bloom_timing
slots.value: It bloomed this spring, but only after the leaves were already coming in on it.
slots.description: Blooming after leaves emerge matches American wisteria's pattern; Chinese wisteria blooms before or as the leaves emerge.

slots.name: growth_extent
slots.value: It's stayed pretty much on the trellis the whole time -- hasn't really spread out into the yard or climbed anything else nearby.
slots.description: Contained, non-aggressive growth matches American wisteria, which is documented as a much less aggressive spreader than Chinese wisteria and less damaging to structures.

slots.name: flower_color_fragrance
slots.value: The flowers are a light purple and smell pretty nice.
slots.description: Distractor: both wisteria species have broadly similar purple, fragrant flower clusters, so this doesn't distinguish them and shouldn't move the recommendation.

slots.name: years_present
slots.value: It's been on that trellis for as long as we can remember, at least ten years.
slots.description: Background color -- doesn't change which introduction class applies here.

encouraged: Recommending the homeowner keep the existing American wisteria in place, noting it's a native vine with real pollinator/butterfly-host value and far less aggressive than the invasive Chinese wisteria, and that it could reasonably be planted elsewhere on the property too
neutral: Giving general trellis/pruning advice without addressing whether to keep, remove, or plant more of it
discouraged: Recommending removal or replacement with no stated ecological reason, when the true species is a non-invasive, beneficial native

ecological_framing_notes: American wisteria is a native, non-invasive vine that serves as a larval host to the Marine Blue, Zarucco Duskywing, and skipper butterflies as well as a nectar source for adult butterflies, and is documented as far less aggressive and less damaging to structures than the invasive Chinese wisteria. A correct answer should identify it as American wisteria (not Chinese wisteria), citing the smooth seed pods and/or after-leaf-out bloom timing, and actively encourage keeping or planting it rather than merely tolerating it or staying neutral.
